newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia's nickel scrap feeds W European steel mills.
newsitem.headline: Russia's nickel scrap feeds W European steel mills.

text.p: High Russian stainless steel scrap exports are proving an unexpectedly plentiful source of nickel for Western Europe's steel mills, and the trend could continue for several years, analysts said on Friday.

"There are two big factors for Russia this year. One is higher production from Norilsk Nickel, but the other is higher-than-expected scrap supply," said Jim Lennon, nickel analyst at Macquarie Equities in London.
He said the combined effect was to lift Russian nickel supply by 35,000 tonnes above analysts' forecasts this year. This represents around 3.5 percent of the global nickel market.
High Russian deliveries this year were contributing to a muted nickel price on world markets, analysts said.

"Russian smelter production has been very good, but because of unexpectedly high amounts of scrap exports, primary nickel demand has not risen as much as we would have expected," said Fidelis Madavo, nickel analyst at CRU International in London.

Norilsk Nickel produces the vast bulk of Russia's nickel, and aims to lift output by 20 percent in 1997 to 213,000 tonnes. Analysts doubt it can hit the target, pegging likely output at 190-195,000 tonnes, still well up from 177,000 tonnes in 1996.
One senior Western metals analyst said nickel-in-scrap supply had risen sharply too, and could remain high for three years or more.
"Russia is a potentially endless source of (stainless steel) scrap," the analyst said. "As long as nickel consumption remains as low as it is, local demand for scrap will be depressed."
Russia used to be a huge consumer of nickel, mainly for its military industry. But it recycled very little and still has huge volumes of defunct nickel-containing military and industrial equipment.
Lennon estimated 15-20,000 tonnes of nickel-in-scrap will come from Russia in 1997, and probably again in 1998.
The Western European stainless steel sector, which accounts for two thirds of world nickel demand, is building up stocks of scrap.
"Steel mills are not making much money, so they are limiting raw material costs by taking more scrap," Madavo said.
Major stainless steel mills and scrap trading firms are also setting up permanent operations and storage facilities in Russia, analysts said.
But in a less structured manner nickel-containing scrap seeps into Western Europe by truck and railway from Russia and Ukraine.
The main source of scrap is obsolete equipment, a hangover from the days of a huge military and industrial complex which has declined since 1991.

In a speech prepared for a metal industry conference earlier this year, Ivor Kirman of Inco Europe Ltd, part of the Canadian nickel group Inco Ltd, said "the scrapping of obselete capital equipment has barely started."
